slides.title: Direct Sign-In boundary
slides.subtitle: Hand authorization to the user's browser, without the model seeing OAuth
slides.notes: Direct Sign-In upgrades a signed-out Session to a signed-in one through the company's own sign-in page. This example covers the first half: everything up to the moment the user's browser opens that page.

slides.title: Why a boundary
slides.statement: The model may **explain** why sign-in is needed. The **host** builds the request.
slides.notes: The agent can tell the user that it needs access to their orders. But the OAuth request, its state and its secrets are built by host code, and the company's page opens in a trusted browser, never inside the conversation.

slides.title: Who takes part
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR M["Model"] subgraph HOST["Your host, trusted"] direction TB H["PAP host
state, verifier, Session Key"] -- "pending request,
hashed state" --> R[("Reactor state store")] end subgraph USR["User's trusted browser"] direction TB B["Browser"] end subgraph CO["Company"] direction TB A["Authorization server
sign-in page"] end M -- "ask for orders:read" --> HOST HOST -- "authorization URL" --> USR USR -- "sign in, S256 challenge" --> CO HOST -. "waiting, scopes, expiry" .-> M
slides.caption: The model asks and is told it is waiting; the URL, state and verifier never leave the host and the browser.
slides.notes: Start with the model: it asks for orders:read on the Session that already exists. Your host does the OAuth work: it makes the state and the PKCE verifier, and keeps the pending request in a Reactor state store, under a hash of the state. It puts the Session Key's thumbprint in the URL as dpop_jkt, so the company binds the code to that Session, and hands the authorization URL only to the user's trusted browser. The browser carries the S256 challenge, never the verifier, to the company's authorization server, where the user signs in and sees the exact scopes. Back to the model, on the dotted line: all it gets is that it is waiting for the user, for which scopes, and until when.

slides.title: Up to the browser

items.title: Derive
items.detail: The S256 challenge; `dpop_jkt`, the Session Key

items.title: Store
items.detail: Pending request by hashed state, with expiry

items.title: Open
items.detail: The authorization URL, in the trusted browser

slides.notes: The host makes a random state and a PKCE verifier, derives the S256 challenge, adds dpop_jkt, the thumbprint of the Session's key, and stores the pending request under a hash of the state, with an expiry. Then it hands the authorization URL to the browser.

slides.title: The whole handoff
slides.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  participant M as Model
  participant H as PAP host
  participant B as Browser
  participant C as Company
  M->>H: Request orders:read
  H->>B: Open authorization URL
  B->>C: Sign-in page
  C-->>B: Authenticate, ask for scopes
  H-->>M: Waiting for user, scopes, expiry
slides.notes: Here is the handoff at once. The model asks, the host opens the company's page in the browser, the company authenticates the user and asks for the scopes, and the model is told only that it is waiting for the user.

slides.title: What the example proves
items: State and verifier come from secure randomness
Only the **S256 challenge** reaches the authorization endpoint, with `dpop_jkt`
The authorization URL is a secret: only the browser handoff sees it
Pending state expires, and can later be consumed atomically
The company owns the sign-in UI: no password reaches the agent
slides.notes: The URL counts as a secret because it carries the state and the user's intent, so only the browser handoff capability ever receives it. Its dpop_jkt binds the code to the Session Key: a code taken from the redirect is useless with any other key, and it signs in this Session and no other. And because the company owns the sign-in page, the agent never sees a password.

slides.title: The pending request
slides.diagram:
stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  state "Pending" as P
  state "Consumed" as C
  state "Expired" as E
  [*] --> P : stored by hashed state
  P --> C : callback, once, atomically
  P --> E : expiry passes
  C --> [*]
  E --> [*]
slides.caption: A pending request is used once or not at all: consumed atomically, or it expires.
slides.notes: This is the one piece of state the host keeps between the browser handoff and the callback. It is stored as pending, under a hash of the state, with an expiry. Later, the callback consumes it exactly once, atomically, so a second callback with the same state finds nothing. If the user never comes back, it expires. Throughout, the authorization URL, the state, the verifier, the user's credentials and the authorization code stay with the host; the model only ever sees waiting, the scopes and the expiry.
